passages.t: ‘Great are the works of the LORD’, and ‘the beginning of wisdom’
passages.happening:
Psalm 111 opens with one word: “Hallelujah!” (verse 1). Then the singer says what he will do. “I will give thanks to the LORD with all my heart in the council of the upright and in the assembly” (verse 1).

The whole psalm is about what God has done. “Great are the works of the LORD; they are pondered by all who delight in them” (verse 2). His work is splendid, and his righteousness lasts forever (verse 3). “He has caused His wonders to be remembered; the LORD is gracious and compassionate” (verse 4).

The singer names the gifts. God gives food to those who fear him and remembers his covenant forever (verse 5). He gave his people a land (verse 6). His commands are trustworthy and stand forever (verses 7 and 8). “He has sent redemption to His people; He has ordained His covenant forever; holy and awesome is His name” (verse 9).

The psalm ends with a saying a wise teacher might give. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom; all who follow His precepts gain rich understanding. His praise endures forever!” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Psalms 111 and 112 are twins. Both begin with ‘Hallelujah’. Both are acrostics, poems that follow the Hebrew alphabet. The book page explains acrostics. In these two, each short line begins with the next of the 22 Hebrew letters. Verses 1 to 8 hold two lines each, and verses 9 and 10 hold three. The pattern is lost in English, but it says something: here is praise from A to Z.

The psalm does not tell the story of the exodus, but a first hearer would catch every hint of it. The ‘wonders’ God made to be remembered (verse 4) point to the rescue from Egypt, and to feasts like Passover that kept it in memory. ‘Food for those who fear Him’ (verse 5) recalls the manna in the desert. The ‘inheritance of the nations’ (verse 6) is the land of Canaan. ‘Redemption’ (verse 9) is the people set free.

‘Gracious and compassionate’ (verse 4) are the words God spoke of himself to Moses on the mountain (Exodus 34:6). They will come back in Psalm 112, and again in Psalm 145.

‘The fear of the LORD’ does not mean being terrified of God. In Israel's wisdom writing it means awe and trust that lead to obedience. It is how a creature rightly stands before the Creator.
passages.later:
The last verse is a saying found more than once in the Bible. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding” (Proverbs 9:10). Proverbs opens with a form of it too (Proverbs 1:7).

Mary sang of God in words close to verse 9: “For the Mighty One has done great things for me. Holy is His name” (Luke 1:49). Zechariah, John the Baptist's father, praised God “because He has visited and redeemed His people” (Luke 1:68).
passages.asks:
Verse 2 says God's works are ‘pondered by all who delight in them’. To ponder is to think slowly and turn a thing over. When did you last stop to think about what God has done, in the Bible's story and in your own?

Notice where wisdom begins. Not with cleverness, or a degree, or experience, but with the fear of the LORD. The psalm asks whether you have begun there.
